title: Spindle Speed (RPM) Calculator
description: Calculate spindle rotational speed based on tooling material cutting speed and diameter.

inputs.name: cuttingSpeed
inputs.label: Cutting Speed (SFM / Vc)
inputs.help: Surface Feet per Minute for specific material and tool coating.

inputs.name: diameter
inputs.label: Cutter Diameter (D)
inputs.help: Nominal diameter of the cutting tool.

formulaExplanation: The RPM equation translates the peripheral linear speed at the cutter's outermost edge (SFM) into rotary speed. Because SFM is given in feet but tool diameter is in inches, we convert feet to inches by multiplying by 12, then divide by π (3.14159) to find the circumference in feet. This simplifies to the constant multiplier 12 / π ≈ 3.82.
engineeringNotes: Always round the RPM down to the nearest safe range if the CNC machine's spindle limit is lower than the computed value. High speed spindles might experience balance and vibration issues; check tool balance specification for ratings exceeding 10,000 RPM.
applications: Setting CNC milling machine spindle speeds
Setting drilling speeds on manual or automatic mills
Calculating speeds for aluminum, steel, and aerospace superalloys

title: Cutting Speed (Vc) Calculator
description: Calculate peripheral linear cutting velocity at the tool outer boundary.

inputs.name: rpm
inputs.label: Spindle Speed (RPM)
inputs.help: Current rotational speed of the spindle.

inputs.name: diameter
inputs.label: Cutter Diameter (D)
inputs.help: Nominal diameter of the cutting tool.

formulaExplanation: Surface Feet per Minute represents how fast the material is moving past the cutting edge. It multiplies the circumference of the tool in inches (Diameter × π) by the RPM, then divides by 12 to convert inches to feet.
engineeringNotes: Selecting the correct surface speed is crucial for tool life. Exceeding recommended SFM increases thermal load dramatically, causing accelerated adhesive or abrasive wear on carbide edges.
applications: Verifying recommended tool life envelopes
Translating Metric catalog specifications (m/min) to Imperial parameters

title: Spindle Torque Calculator
description: Determine the torque exerted by the spindle motor for a given power and speed.

inputs.name: horsepower
inputs.label: Motor Power (HP)
inputs.help: Active output power at the spindle shaft.

inputs.name: rpm
inputs.label: Spindle Speed (RPM)
inputs.help: Spindle rotational speed.

formulaExplanation: Torque and Power are related through rotational velocity. The constant 5252 is derived from converting horsepower (33,000 ft-lb/min) to foot-pounds per radian-second (divided by 2π).
engineeringNotes: Electric induction spindle motors lose torque dramatically at low speeds unless coupled with a mechanical gearbox. Ensure your roughing cuts are within the spindle's flat-torque RPM range.
applications: Verifying spindle motor capabilities for heavy steel roughing
Sizing gear ratios or belts for custom machine builds

title: Spindle Power Calculator
description: Calculate actual power consumption during material removal.

inputs.name: torqueNm
inputs.label: Spindle Torque (N·m)
inputs.help: Torque being exerted by the cutter tool edge.

inputs.name: rpm
inputs.label: Spindle Speed (RPM)
inputs.help: Active shaft rotational velocity.

formulaExplanation: This computes power from rotary parameters. We first convert Torque in N·m to lb-ft (by dividing by 1.3558), then multiply by RPM, and divide by 5252.
engineeringNotes: Total power drawn from the wall is always higher due to motor inefficiency, axis drivers, pump systems, and friction. Factor in an 85% mechanical efficiency constraint.
applications: Determining power demand limits on workshop electrical service
Optimizing heavy tool paths without tripping breaker limits

title: Spindle Bearing Life (L10)
description: Predict the nominal fatigue lifespan of rolling element bearings in hours.

inputs.name: dynamicLoad
inputs.label: Dynamic Rating (C)
inputs.help: Manufacturer rating for bearing dynamic capacity.

inputs.name: radialLoad
inputs.label: Equivalent Load (P)
inputs.help: Estimated working load during machining cuts.

inputs.name: rpm
inputs.label: Spindle Speed (RPM)
inputs.help: Weighted average spindle RPM.

formulaExplanation: L10 life represents the period that 90% of a group of identical bearings will survive without material fatigue. The formula scales the ratio of structural capacity (C) vs operating load (P) raised to the exponent of 3 (for ball bearings; roller bearings use 10/3), adjusted for rotational speed in hours.
engineeringNotes: Heavy cutting forces, tool unbalance, and excessive preloads generate radial stresses that severely curtail spindle bearing lifespan. Keep cutting forces within 10-15% of the dynamic rating to ensure decades of spindle operation.
applications: CNC spindle custom building and sizing
Predictive preventive maintenance schedules for machining cells

title: Spindle Thermal Expansion
description: Determine how much a spindle shaft, machine column or workpiece grows due to thermal gradients.

inputs.name: length
inputs.label: Original Length (L)
inputs.help: Unconstrained dimension length at reference temperature.

inputs.name: tempDiff
inputs.label: Temp Change (ΔT)
inputs.help: Temperature difference relative to standard environment (68°F / 20°C).

inputs.name: coeff
inputs.label: Coeff α (×10⁻⁶ /°F)
inputs.help: Thermal coefficient of expansion (e.g. Aluminum: 13.0, Steel: 6.5, Carbide: 3.1).

formulaExplanation: The change in length is directly proportional to the original dimension, the temperature difference, and the material's structural coefficient of thermal expansion.
engineeringNotes: Thermal drift is the leading cause of geometric accuracy issues on high-precision CNC mills. A 24" aluminum part heated by 15°F expands by nearly 0.005 inches, exceeding critical tolerances instantly.
applications: Workpiece sizing corrections in variable climates
Estimating machine spindle thermal growth during long shifts

title: Surface Speed Calculator
description: Convert spindle rotation into the true linear rim velocity at the cutter periphery, in imperial and metric units simultaneously.
formulaExplanation: The peripheral surface speed equals the cutter circumference (π × D) multiplied by rotational frequency, normalized to feet per minute. This instrument will display both SFM and m/min with live conversion.
engineeringNotes: Surface speed is the governing variable in tool vendor catalogs. Verify that the chosen rim velocity stays within the coating's thermal envelope for the workpiece alloy.
applications: Cross-checking drilling and milling setups between imperial and metric shops
Sizing rim-speed-limits for grinding wheel peripherals

title: Spindle Runout Tolerance
description: Budget the allowable Total Indicated Runout for a toolholder assembly given diameter, RPM and finish requirements.
formulaExplanation: Runout tolerance scales the permissible indicator reading against target finish — cosmetically critical cuts demand runout below 0.0002 in, while heavy roughing tolerates 0.0005 in or more.
engineeringNotes: Always measure TIR at the cutting flute, not the shank: deflection and collet distortion compound gauge length errors.
applications: Qualifying collet chucks after a spindle crash
Setting acceptance criteria for HSK and CAT assemblies

title: Angular Acceleration
description: Compute the angular acceleration a spindle drive must deliver to reach target RPM within a commanded duration.
formulaExplanation: Constant-velocity ramp kinematics: the angular acceleration in rad/s² is the angular velocity delta divided by ramp time. This feeds directly into spindle inertia torque budgeting.
engineeringNotes: Drives derate peak current at high duty; verify the acceleration demand sits inside the 2-second peak-torque window of the spindle amplifier.
applications: Programming rigid-tapping spindle ramping
Sizing energy consumption for high-inertia mill drums

title: Spindle Moment of Inertia
description: Calculate the rotational inertia of solid and hollow cylindrical spindle shafts, chucks and workpiece drums.
formulaExplanation: For a uniform solid cylinder of density ρ, length L and diameter D, polar inertia scales with the fourth power of diameter. Hollow variants subtract the inner-bore inertia term.
engineeringNotes: Inertia grows with D⁴ — a doubling of chuck diameter increases stored rotational energy sixteen-fold, demanding substantially longer ramp windows.
applications: Estimating spindle run-up energy on large 4-jaw chucks
Balancing rotary table drum inertia against drive ratings

title: Table Feed Rate Calculator
description: Calculate the linear table translation feed rate for milling and drilling operations.

inputs.name: rpm
inputs.label: Spindle Speed (RPM)
inputs.help: Active spindle rotational speed.

inputs.name: flutes
inputs.label: Number of Flutes (Z)
inputs.help: The number of active cutting teeth on the tool.

inputs.name: feedPerTooth
inputs.label: Feed per Tooth (Fz)
inputs.help: The desired chip thickness cut by a single flute.

formulaExplanation: The total linear distance traversed by the machine table in one minute is the RPM multiplied by the number of cutting teeth, multiplied by the thickness of the chip carved by each tooth.
engineeringNotes: Too low of a feed rate causes rubbing, rubbing work-hardens stainless alloys and burns wood/plastics. Too high of a feed rate exceeds tool strength, causing instantaneous breaking.
applications: Generating CNC feed codes (G01 F values)
Estimating overall machining throughput and machine loads

title: Feed per Tooth (Fz)
description: Derive the nominal cutting advance per flute from an existing setup.

inputs.name: feedRate
inputs.label: Table Feed Rate (F)
inputs.help: Measured linear machine table travel velocity.

inputs.name: rpm
inputs.label: Spindle Speed (RPM)
inputs.help: Rotational speed of the spindle.

inputs.name: flutes
inputs.label: Number of Flutes (Z)
inputs.help: Number of cutting teeth on the tool.

formulaExplanation: This is the inverse of the feed rate calculator. It divides the linear speed by the total teeth engaging the material per minute to check if the cutting edge is properly cutting versus rubbing.
engineeringNotes: Compare this resulting chip load against the manufacturer's tool catalog. For miniature cutters (< 0.050"), chip loads are often in the ten-thousandths (0.0002" - 0.0005").
applications: Reverse engineering CAM outputs
Troubleshooting broken tool occurrences

title: Feed per Revolution
description: Convert chip-load-per-tooth into the full rotational advance per spindle revolution used by turning and drilling cycles.
formulaExplanation: Feed per revolution sums the individual tooth chip loads across all cutting edges — the standard unit used by lathe G99 cycles and drilling canned routines.
engineeringNotes: For single-point turning tools Z = 1, so feed/rev equals the edge chip load. Multi-insert drills divide the aggregate advance across inserts.
applications: Programming G99 lathe cycles directly
Converting drill catalog feed-per-rev tables into IPM

title: Material Removal Rate (MRR)
description: Measure the volume of material carved away per unit time.

inputs.name: radialDepth
inputs.label: Radial Depth of Cut (Ae)
inputs.help: Width of cut engagement normal to feed.

inputs.name: axialDepth
inputs.label: Axial Depth of Cut (Ap)
inputs.help: Depth of cut along tool axis direction.

inputs.name: feedRate
inputs.label: Table Feed Rate (F)
inputs.help: Linear table feed speed.

formulaExplanation: MRR represents volumetric output. It is the rectangular cross-sectional area of the cut (Radial width Ae × Axial height Ap) multiplied by the travel speed (Feed Rate F).
engineeringNotes: MRR is the best proxy for required spindle horsepower. As a rule of thumb, cutting steel requires roughly 1 HP per cubic inch per minute, whereas aluminum requires 0.3 HP per cubic inch per minute.
applications: Optimizing roughing strategies and pocketing CAM parameters
Estimating cycle throughput for massive batch productions

title: Chip Load Calculator
description: Calculate true chip thickness when the radial engagement width (Ae) is less than half the tool diameter.

inputs.name: feedPerTooth
inputs.label: Nominal Chip Load (Fz)
inputs.help: Nominal catalog feed per tooth.

inputs.name: diameter
inputs.label: Tool Diameter (D)
inputs.help: Full cutter outer diameter.

inputs.name: radialDepth
inputs.label: Radial Depth (Ae)
inputs.help: Radial stepover engagement value.

formulaExplanation: When radial engagement (Ae) is small (< 50% diameter), the cutter tooth exits the material before forming a full-thickness chip. The physical chip thickness is actually thinner than the feed-per-tooth. To maintain true chip thickness and avoid rubbing, the feed rate must be increased by the thinning compensation factor.
engineeringNotes: High-efficiency milling (HEM) paths rely heavily on chip thinning. Without compensation, the tool will rub and work-harden the material, leading to dramatic thermal failure of the carbide.
applications: High Efficiency Milling (HEM) and dynamic toolpaths in CAM
Adjusting feed rates for very light radial finish passes

title: Depth of Cut Optimization
description: Balance axial depth against available spindle power and machine rigidity to maximize volumetric removal without deflection failure.
formulaExplanation: Optimized depth resolves the power equation P = Kp × Ae × Ap × Vc against the spindle's continuous rating, then derates for L/D tool rigidity and workpiece fixture stiffness.
engineeringNotes: Prefer deep-axial/low-stepover strategies on rigid machines; favor shallow-axial/high-stepover on gantry routers and lightweight VMCs.
applications: Planning heavy roughing passes on 1018 steel frames
Distributing roughing passes for thin-web aluminum plates

title: Width of Cut Calculator
description: Compute the radial engagement width from target cusp heights, engagement angle, or scallop geometry on contour passes.
formulaExplanation: The chordal width under a round cutter of diameter D and residual cusp height h follows circle geometry. Instrument supports direct width, engagement-angle and cusp-height driven modes.
engineeringNotes: Match radial width against flute length and coolant reach before committing to deep periphery passes on high-tensile alloys.
applications: Setting stepovers for ball-nose 3D finishing
Verifying engagement width for slot clearing with roughers

title: Cutting Time Calculator
description: Calculate theoretical cutting time for a single-pass milling, turning, or drilling operation.

inputs.name: length
inputs.label: Length of Cut (L)
inputs.help: Total linear feed length, including approach and overtravel.

inputs.name: feedRate
inputs.label: Table Feed Rate (F)
inputs.help: Linear feeding speed of the cutter.

inputs.name: auxTime
inputs.label: Auxiliary Time (T_aux)
inputs.help: Time for tool changes, rapids, fixtures, and operator adjustments.

formulaExplanation: The cutting duration is the length divided by speed, plus secondary times. T_aux represents manual or rapid functions parsed in seconds, converted to minutes.
engineeringNotes: To optimize high volume production, minimizing tool-to-tool rapid duration (auxTime) is often as valuable as squeezing cutting feeds.
applications: Quoting milling jobs for machine shop bidding
Estimating battery or power usage profiles for small-batch CNC series

title: Surface Finish Calculator
description: Calculate theoretical average surface roughness (Ra) for a turning nose insert.

inputs.name: feedRate
inputs.label: Feed Rate per Rev (f)
inputs.help: Linear table feed advance per spindle revolution.

inputs.name: noseRadius
inputs.label: Tool Nose Radius (R)
inputs.help: Corner radius of the carbide turning insert.

formulaExplanation: As a round nose tool traverses a cylinder, it leaves microscopic cusps. Theoretical height is a function of the pitch squared divided by the geometry. Dividing by 32 and scaling translates the geometric height into center-line average roughness (Ra).
engineeringNotes: Real surface finishes are often 20-50% rougher due to material tearing, chatter, and micro-edge chipping. If the finish is poor, increase the insert nose radius or slow down feed speed (f).
applications: Selecting feed rates for precise final cosmetic turning operations
Sizing insert index labels for aerospace finish cuts

title: Tool Engagement Calculator
description: Evaluate the cutter-to-workpiece engagement angle from radial depth and diameter — the true driver of force spikes in slotting.
formulaExplanation: Engagement angle grows from near-0° at hairline stepovers to 180° at full slot width. Cutting force, heat flux and flute entry stress scale roughly linearly with this angle.
engineeringNotes: Keep engagement below 90-120° for weak setups; above 150° expect doubled cutting forces and enter chipping risk territory on ceramics.
applications: Auditing CAM slotting passes for force spikes
Designing safe toolpaths for cast-iron interrupted cuts

title: Tool Life (Taylor Equation)
description: Model expected cutter life in minutes from cutting speed using the classic Taylor tool-life relationship.
formulaExplanation: Taylor's empirical law links surface speed V to tool life T via material constants C and exponent n (HSS ≈ 0.08-0.13, carbide ≈ 0.2-0.5, ceramic ≈ 0.5-0.7). Slight speed hikes collapse life exponentially.
engineeringNotes: Validate constants against the insert datasheet; coolant delivery and chip evacuation can swing real-life results by ±40% around the Taylor prediction.
applications: Choosing economically-optimal SFM for lights-out batches
Estimating insert replacement frequency for cost models

title: Ball Screw Critical Speed
description: Calculate the first resonant frequency (whirling speed) limit of linear actuator ball screws.

inputs.name: diameter
inputs.label: Root Diameter (d)
inputs.help: Diameter measured at the root of the ball track.

inputs.name: length
inputs.label: Unsupported Length (L)
inputs.help: Maximum span between support bearings.

inputs.name: mountFactor
inputs.label: Mounting Constant (Cf)
inputs.help: Support arrangement: Fixed-Supported is 2.23, Fixed-Fixed is 3.92, Fixed-Free is 0.36.

formulaExplanation: Whirling occurs when the rotational velocity matches the screw shaft's bending resonance. This speed is directly proportional to screw root diameter and the support bearing configuration constant, but inversely proportional to the square of unsupported length.
engineeringNotes: Exceeding critical speed causes severe lateral vibration, destroying ballnuts and accuracy. Design axes to operate below 80% of critical speed limit.
applications: Sizing CNC linear axis drive components
Designing long stroke routing machine drive lines

title: Ball Screw Buckling Load
description: Determine the maximum axial compressive load a mounted screw shaft can carry before elastic column buckling.
formulaExplanation: Euler's column formula applies directly: end-fixity factor K ranges from 0.25 (fixed-free) to 4.0 (fixed-fixed), and the root-diameter second moment I governs resistance.
engineeringNotes: Compressive loads mainly occur on the stroke that drives the nut away from the drive end. Always derate for 2-3× safety where heavy Z-axis gantries bury the screw.
applications: Verifying screw diameter for vertical axis weight bearing
Sizing screws against peak cutting-force thrust

title: Ball Screw Torque
description: Convert required linear thrust force into rotary drive torque at the screw coupling, including efficiency losses.
formulaExplanation: Thrust F delivered through a screw of given lead at efficiency η (ground screws ≈ 0.90, rolled ≈ 0.80) sets the continuous coupling torque the servo must sustain.
engineeringNotes: Include guideway preload drag in F — nominally 15-25% additional thrust on heavily-preloaded profile rails.
applications: Sizing direct-coupled servo torque margins
Checking T-handle muscle effort on manual positioning tables

title: Ball Screw Efficiency
description: Estimate ball screw mechanical efficiency from lead angle and contact friction — and verify backdrivability margins.
formulaExplanation: Lead angle λ versus friction angle φ sets forward efficiency. Efficiency above ~50% makes the screw backdrivable; Z-axes then require counterbalance or braking.
engineeringNotes: Rolled screws with aggressive preloads lose 5-15% efficiency heat-wise at high duty cycles; monitor nut temperature on repetitive rapid tests.
applications: Selecting Z axis brakes on vertical machining centers
Evaluating manual backdrivability for setup-friendly routers

title: Ball Screw Life
description: Predict expected screw-nut fatigue life in revolutions and travel kilometers under mean working loads.
formulaExplanation: Analogous to bearing L10 life: dynamic capacity ratio cubed sets revolutions; multiply by lead to obtain life in distance traveled.
engineeringNotes: Load histograms matter — a mean-load approximation with weighted duty percentages yields dramatically more honest figures than peak-load estimates.
applications: Forecasting screw replacement intervals on 24/7 gantry cells
Justifying preloaded double-nut upgrades in quoting documents

title: Linear Speed Calculator
description: Translate motor RPM and screw lead into actual axis travel velocity in m/min and ipm.
formulaExplanation: One revolution advances the lead distance; dividing the per-minute product by 60 yields per-second velocity. Instrument displays both unit systems simultaneously.
engineeringNotes: Verify computed rapid speed stays below the screw's DN-limit (diameter × RPM) as well as the linear guide velocity rating.
applications: Confirming router gantry rapid velocity settings
Converting between controller feedrate displays and motor tachometers

title: Axis Acceleration
description: Compute axis acceleration ramps in m/s² and G-forces from commanded velocity and ramp window.
formulaExplanation: Linear trapezoidal profile: sustained acceleration equals the velocity delta divided by ramp time. Outputs include G-equivalents for operator/slosh intuition.
engineeringNotes: Past ~0.5 G, workpiece fixtures and coolant sloshing become limiting — not the motor. Verify table-clamping force under peak acceleration.
applications: Tuning jerk-limited S-curve profiles
Validating vacuum fixture holding power during brisk starts

title: Linear Inertia
description: Reflect translating table and workpiece mass into equivalent rotary inertia at the screw coupling.
formulaExplanation: Every kilogram of linear mass maps onto the rotary shaft through the squared lead arm. Add screw self-inertia and coupling terms for the total drive inertia.
engineeringNotes: Heavy workpieces change axis dynamics batch-to-batch; verify the load-inertia/rotor ratio stays inside 10:1 across the full pallet mix.
applications: Servo sizing for heavy gantry portals
Estimating impact inertia of 200 kg vise assemblies

title: Positioning Accuracy
description: Score axis positioning accuracy and repeatability from a bidirectional laser-interferometer measurement series.
formulaExplanation: VDI 3441-style scoring: accuracy is the largest deviation of the mean position from target; repeatability is the spread band of reversal-measured approaches.
engineeringNotes: Always approach targets from one direction before reversal measurements — conceal-direction shifts inflate the apparent accuracy metric unrealistically.
applications: Acceptance testing new machining centers
Annual ISO 230 verification of production routers

title: Backlash Compensation
description: Compute controller backlash compensation values from dial-indicator reversal measurements taken along the axis.
formulaExplanation: Measure the reversal deadband at several axis stations; the controller injects the mean value when direction changes. Output gives masked and signed entries for common controllers.
engineeringNotes: Compensating more than ~0.03 mm of mechanical slop hides a failing nut — replace worn preloads rather than masking them digitally.
applications: Entering machine-parameter backlash tables after warm-up
Auditing reversal spikes on machined circles

title: Servo Motor Sizing
description: Evaluate required servo shaft torque to accelerate inertia and overcome slide friction.

inputs.name: inertia
inputs.label: Rotational Inertia (J)
inputs.help: Sum of motor rotor, screw shaft, and linear table translated inertia.

inputs.name: acceleration
inputs.label: Angular Accel (α)
inputs.help: Peak rotational acceleration requested during rapids.

inputs.name: friction
inputs.label: Friction Torque (T_f)
inputs.help: Torque needed to overcome guideway seal friction and slide preload.

formulaExplanation: The motor must generate enough force to accelerate the rotating and linear masses (Inertia J × Acceleration α) in addition to overcoming static and dynamic friction of slides and bearings.
engineeringNotes: Always select a servo with a continuous torque rating exceeding your friction requirements, and a peak acceleration torque that satisfies this total load with a 20-30% safety margin.
applications: Selecting closed-loop AC servo motors for axis upgrades
Tuning feedback PID loops for CNC gantry acceleration

title: Required Motor Torque
description: Aggregate continuous torque demand: friction drag, cutting-force thrust through the lead, and gravitational lift (Z-axis).
formulaExplanation: Continuous torque stacks friction, thrust-reflected cutting loads, and gravity lift. Unlike the peak sizing calculator, this focuses on thermal continuous-duty checks.
engineeringNotes: Keep computed value below 60% of motor continuous torque for headroom against warm-room semiconductors derating.
applications: Verifying Z servo sizing without counterbalance
Selecting motor frames for horizontal heavy-load axes

title: Reflected Inertia
description: Map gearbox downstream inertia back onto the motor shaft through the squared gear ratio.
formulaExplanation: Division by GR² lets massive table inertia appear trivial at the motor — the reason belt reducers transform dynamic response for large gantries.
engineeringNotes: A 5:1 reducer swaps 25× inertia advantage for 5× output speed loss. Choose ratio against required rapid speed first, then verify inertia ratio ≤ 10:1.
applications: Pairing belt reducers with gantry X-axes
Evaluating direct-drive versus geared screw arrangements

title: Gear Ratio Calculator
description: Derive belt or gear reduction ratio from motor speed and desired screw RPM, including pulley-tooth counting helpers.
formulaExplanation: Simple rotation ratio — with auxiliary modes to convert tooth counts between timing pulleys and to expose output shaft characteristics.
engineeringNotes: Timing belts: keep small pulleys ≥ 16 teeth to avoid belt-flex fatigue and positional wind-up under reversing loads.
applications: Designing Z-axis 2:1 belt stages
Mapping rotary table worm reducer choices

title: Acceleration Torque
description: Isolate the pure dynamic torque component needed to accelerate the total coupled drivetrain inertia.
formulaExplanation: Accelerating torque is inertia × angular acceleration alone — no friction or gravity terms — used when sizing the motor's short-time peak capabilities.
engineeringNotes: Motor peak windows are typically 2-3× continuous for a few seconds; verify motor datasheets support your fastest commanded acceleration.
applications: Confirming aggressive flag linkage approaches
Documenting peak current demand for drive tuning

title: RMS Torque
description: Compute the thermally-weighted root-mean-square torque across a full motion duty cycle — the true motor heat check.
formulaExplanation: Duty cycles square each torque segment before averaging, so brief high-torque peaks matter less than sustained heavy thrust. Compare to motor continuous rating.
engineeringNotes: Target T_rms ≤ 80% of continuous-rated torque at your worst-case ambient machine-enclosure temperature.
applications: Approving high-feed cycles of engraving heads
Documenting thermal duty for linear motor stages

title: Holding Torque
description: Determine stall torque requirements to keep backdrivable axes motionless under gravity and fixture loads during e-stops.
formulaExplanation: Static equilibrium torque for vertical/backdrivable axes — motor must hold without current overheating, alternatively a mechanical brake matches half this value.
engineeringNotes: Electromagnetic brakes usually rate to hold 150% of computed gravity torque across wear life; never rely on holding torque alone for personnel safety.
applications: Specifying Z brakes on bridge mills
Sizing counterbalance cylinders for vertical portals

title: Motor Power Requirement
description: Calculate continuous kilowatts a servo must deliver based on RMS torque at the sustained operating speed.
formulaExplanation: Mechanical power is torque × angular velocity. Instrument converts to kW and HP, then suggests nearest standard motor frame power classes.
engineeringNotes: Size against the RMS floor plus 25% margin — servo ratings assume 40°C ambient; hot enclosures push derating curves down by 10-15%.
applications: Specifying VFD service capacity for multi-axis cells
Cross-checking vendor axis-drive selections before purchase

title: Regenerative Energy
description: Estimate kinetic energy returned to the DC bus during deceleration and the braking-resistor power it implies.
formulaExplanation: Decelerating inertia dumps rotational kinetic energy back into the drive bus. Instrument reports joules-per-stop and average wattage at your cycle frequency.
engineeringNotes: Gantry portals with 300+ kg tables need significant braking resistance at 0.5 G decel; measure bus capacitance and resistor thermal limits before tuning hard stops.
applications: Sizing external braking resistors for Z axis
Comparing DC-bus sharing architectures for multi-axis machines

title: Servo Speed Calculator
description: Convert commanded linear axis velocity into motor shaft RPM through screw lead and gear reduction.
formulaExplanation: Linear speed divided by lead gives screw RPM; multiplied by any gearbox ratio yields motor shaft speed. Verifies axis feed demands sit inside motor speed ranges.
engineeringNotes: Keep sustained motor RPM below the drive's continuous field-weakening boundary to preserve torque fidelity through long cuts.
applications: Checking whether 30 m/min rapids exceed motor ratings
Setting spindle pulley stages for high-speed mill drums

title: Tool Deflection
description: Analyze elastic bending deflection at the tool tip under radial cutting loads.

inputs.name: force
inputs.label: Radial Cutting Force (F)
inputs.help: Radial mechanical force push against cutter shank.

inputs.name: overhang
inputs.label: Tool Overhang (L)
inputs.help: Distance from tool holder face to cutting tip.

inputs.name: diameter
inputs.label: Tool Shank Diameter (D)
inputs.help: Shank diameter of the tool.

inputs.name: modulus
inputs.label: Elastic Modulus (E ×10⁶)
inputs.help: Modulus of elasticity. Carbide ≈ 87-93 Mpsi, Steel/HSS ≈ 30 Mpsi.

formulaExplanation: The cutter acts as a cantilever beam with a point load. Deflection equals Force × Overhang cubed, divided by three times the Elastic Modulus × Area Moment of Inertia. Because tool diameter is in the denominator to the 4th power (I = πD⁴/64), deflection is highly sensitive to tool diameter and overhang.
engineeringNotes: An increase in overhang dramatically blows up deflection (by a factor of L³). Keep the tool choked up as high as possible in the collet. If you double the tool diameter, you reduce deflection sixteenfold!
applications: Estimating wall taper error on deep pocket profiling
Selecting appropriate shank materials (solid carbide vs steel shanks)

title: Tool Overhang
description: Score overhang length-to-diameter ratio and estimate its direct effect on vibration risk and finish degradation.
formulaExplanation: L/D ≤ 3 is conservative; 3-5 demands tuned feeds; beyond 6 requires anti-vibration damped bars. Instrument reports ratio bands and the √(L³) deflection amplification.
engineeringNotes: Do not confuse gauge projection with usable cutting depth — a 10 mm effective reach with 60 mm overhang machines like the longer stickout.
applications: Auditing CAM tooling lists before purchasing long-reach drills
Comparing shrink-fit versus side-lock holder projections

title: Tool Pull Force
description: Compute drawbar clamping force requirements and translatable breakout safety margins for steep-taper tooling.
formulaExplanation: Drawbar springs generate axial force; taper contact friction multiplies it into holding effectiveness. Instrument compares working clamp force against peak cutting ejection vectors.
engineeringNotes: Never machine above 70% of rated drawbar pull — loss of grip causes tool drop-in crashes. Clean tapers improve contact efficiency by 5-8%.
applications: Verifying heavy face-mill grip on CAT-40 tapers
Investigating tool-ejection incidents after crashes

title: HSK Taper Contact
description: Estimate the percentage of hollow-shank taper surface in contact based on combined tolerances of spindle and holder.
formulaExplanation: HSK relies on simultaneous face + taper contact; bi-metal tolerance stacking shrinks effective surface area, dropping stiffness that HSK's dual-interface design promises.
engineeringNotes: Under 75% contact area, chatter marks emerge even at conservative speeds; verify gauge readings with blue-contact compound checks.
applications: Qualifying new HSK-A63 holder batches
Diagnosing unexplained taper fretting corrosion

title: Tool Holder Balance Grade
description: Convert measured residual unbalance mass-eccentricity into ISO 1940 balance quality grades (G-values).
formulaExplanation: Balance quality G is specific unbalance × angular velocity — a G6.3 holder at 20,000 RPM tolerates roughly G50 worth of eccentricity at 2,800 RPM. Assemblies must sum holder + tool + retention knob.
engineeringNotes: High-speed spindles (>12,000 RPM) demand assemblies at G2.5 or better; adding cutting tools after balancing often invalidates published holder grades.
applications: Preparing assemblies for 20k RPM mold machines
Diagnosing 1×RPM vibration signatures in spindles

title: Tool Weight
description: Estimate assembled tool weight from material density and geometric volume for ATC balance and magazine load planning.
formulaExplanation: Cylindrical approximation of the cutting body plus holder mass gives magazine load; instrument consecutively compares against the ATC's maximum tool payload rating.
engineeringNotes: Large boring assemblies exceed many magazine limits — verify ATC payload before programming auto-changes on heavy parts.
applications: Confirming heavy face mills fit magazine ratings
Predicting unbalance shifts when interchanging assembly components

title: Tool Center Point (TCP)
description: Resolve five-axis TCP offsets: holder length, gauge length and TCL (Tool Center-point control) compensation values.
formulaExplanation: Trunnion machines rotate about physical axes; TCP compensation needs exact machine-kinematic offsets so the control can keep the tool tip stationary while tilting.
engineeringNotes: Registering wrong gauge lengths by even 0.05 mm shows up as matched-surface seams in 3+2 machining — always re-probe moving-drums after holder swaps.
applications: Setting TCP tables for DMU trunnion cells
Verifying tool gauge-length deviation after sharpening

title: Tool Stick-Out Calculator
description: Determine safe clamp depth and exposed flute projection ensuring the cutting depth fits inside the secure gauged stick-out.
formulaExplanation: Considers required cutting reach, flute length and a collision clearance bucket to find the safe exposed projection; warns when collet lands too far up the flute roots.
engineeringNotes: Never clamp on flute geometry — helical relief mouths rupture under collet squeeze and throw radial runout into tenths of millimeters.
applications: Presetting deep-reach bores
Validating endmill grip depth in ER collets

title: Tool Change Time
description: Model full ATC cycle time: spindle retreat, carousel index, gripper swap and return-to-cut positioning.
formulaExplanation: Decomposes an automatic tool change into mechanical stages so operators can see where cycle budget bleeds — carousel wobble usually dominates slower than gripper actuation.
engineeringNotes: Random-access magazines with servo carousel indexing reclaim 1-2 seconds per change over sequential nearest-neighbor search patterns.
applications: Trimming 200-part batch times through tool-order optimization
Rating umbrella vs arm-type ATC designs

title: Tool Magazine Capacity Estimator
description: Estimate effective carousel pocket count given tool diameters, pocket pitch, and large-tool adjacent-pocket clearing rules.
formulaExplanation: Big face mills demand empty neighboring pockets; the estimator maps real tool diameters to occupied slots, exposing honest usable capacity versus advertised count.
engineeringNotes: Validate combined pocket weights — a full 24-tool magazine of 3 kg holders can exceed carousel torque and indexing system ratings.
applications: Planning tooling layouts for unattended machining
Sizing magazine upgrades for high-mix job shops
